lesson.title: Breakpoints: Pausing Time Inside Your Program
lesson.summary: A breakpoint marks a specific line where the debugger pauses execution so you can inspect variables, the call stack, and program flow at that exact moment.
lesson.body:
A breakpoint marks a specific line in your code where you want the program to pause, so you can inspect its state at that exact moment instead of guessing what it must be based on the final output. You set one by clicking in the margin next to a line number in your editor, or with a keyboard shortcut; a small marker, usually a red dot, appears to show it is active. When you run the program in debug mode, execution proceeds completely normally until it reaches that line, at which point it freezes: no further code runs until you tell the debugger to continue.

This matters because it lets you choose exactly where to look, rather than pausing everywhere or nowhere. Picture a program that processes a list of thirty student scores and crashes on one specific value partway through. Setting a breakpoint on the line that processes each score would work, but the debugger would pause thirty times, once per student, and you would have to click continue over and over just to reach the one that actually causes the problem. This is where a conditional breakpoint helps: most debuggers let you attach a condition to a breakpoint, such as score is not an int, so the debugger only pauses when that condition is true. Instead of stepping through twenty nine irrelevant students, execution runs normally until it hits the exact iteration where the score is, say, the string "95" instead of the integer 95, and pauses there, with every variable at that moment available for inspection.

This is a clear improvement over print debugging for this kind of case. A plain print statement inside that loop would print all thirty scores, giving you output to scroll through and compare by eye; a conditional breakpoint gives you only the one moment that matters, already paused, with the full state visible in the debugger's variables pane instead of scattered across console output.

Breakpoints are the foundation the rest of a debugger's tools build on. Once execution is paused at one, you can inspect variables, look at the call stack, or begin stepping through the code one line at a time, which is exactly what the next chapter covers.
